sections.heading: Thanking you for bringing me near
sections.text: Father, I am blessed because you have called me to yourself. With you there is mercy, freedom, forgiveness, and real confidence before you. You did not leave me trapped in my sin. You brought me out, declared me forgiven, and gave my conscience rest. Through faith in Christ, you have made peace with me and welcomed me into the freedom of being your child.
theological_themes: God graciously chooses and calls his people to himself.
Forgiveness and redemption free the sinner from guilt and bondage.
Justification by faith brings peace with God and assurance in the conscience.
Adoption gives the believer the freedom and security of belonging to God as Father.

scripture_references.connection: This psalm blesses the person whom God chooses and brings near to dwell with him, which directly supports the prayer’s opening gratitude for God’s initiative in calling a sinner to himself.
Paul teaches that being justified by faith results in peace with God through Jesus Christ, grounding the prayer’s confidence that God has declared the believer right with him.
This passage connects the Spirit’s work with the believer’s adoption and assurance, supporting the prayer’s language of liberty as God’s child and a conscience settled before him.

sections.heading: Asking to be kept from false confidence
sections.text: Please keep me from fooling myself with a faith that only looks alive on the outside. Do not let me assume I belong to Christ if I am unchanged. Do not let me claim the Spirit’s life while my mind and desires are still ruled by the flesh. Do not let me be satisfied with religious words, habits, or services if my heart is not truly turned toward you.
theological_themes: There is a real danger of hypocritical religion and false assurance.
True union with Christ produces a new life, not merely outward profession.
The Spirit’s presence is shown by a changed mind, desires, and direction.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes those who are in Christ as a new creation, which grounds the prayer’s refusal to treat an unchanged life as evidence of real saving faith.
This passage contrasts the mind set on the flesh with the mind set on the Spirit and says that belonging to Christ is inseparable from the Spirit’s presence and rule.
Jesus warns that religious claims and visible works can exist without true obedience to the Father, supporting the prayer’s concern about outward religion without a heart right with God.

sections.heading: Learning how to recognize a sincere heart
sections.text: Teach me to examine myself honestly before you. Let me not measure sincerity by how much I say, how much I know, or how religious I appear. Let me look for the marks you care about: a real fear of grieving you, a serious desire to know what pleases you, and a willingness to say no to myself in order to follow Christ.
theological_themes: Self-examination must be done before God, not for self-display.
Sincere faith shows itself in reverence, obedience, and teachability.
Following Christ includes self-denial.

scripture_references.connection: The psalmist asks God to search and lead him, giving biblical shape to the prayer’s request for honest self-examination before God.
Jesus connects love for him with keeping his commandments, supporting the prayer’s desire to judge sincerity by a heart that wants to obey God.
Jesus says discipleship requires denying oneself and following him, which directly grounds the prayer’s request for willingness to give up self-rule for Christ.

sections.heading: Keeping your glory and commands before me
sections.text: Do not let anything make me forget your glory. Do not let anything pull me away from your commands, weaken my trust in your promises, or cause harm to your people. Guard my life so that my choices do not become a stumbling block to other believers.
theological_themes: God’s glory should govern the believer’s priorities and conduct.
Obedience and trust in God’s promises belong together.
Love for fellow believers includes care not to wound or mislead them.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that even ordinary actions are to be done for God’s glory, supporting the prayer’s desire that nothing eclipse God’s honor.
The psalmist seeks God with the whole heart and treasures his word in order not to sin, fitting the prayer’s request not to be turned aside from God’s commands.
Paul warns believers not to put a stumbling block before one another, grounding the prayer’s concern not to offend or harm God’s children.

sections.heading: Not letting daily life crowd out what matters most
sections.text: Keep my work, responsibilities, plans, and ordinary concerns from damaging my life with you. Help me handle what is necessary without letting it take over my heart. Do not let the pressure and noise of life make me neglect the one thing I most need: to sit before you, listen to you, and live in fellowship with you.
theological_themes: Ordinary responsibilities are good but can become spiritually distracting.
The kingdom of God must remain the believer’s first priority.
Communion with Christ is more necessary than anxious busyness.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus commends Mary’s attention to him over Martha’s anxious busyness, illuminating the prayer’s phrase about not neglecting the one thing needful.

Jesus calls his disciples away from anxious preoccupation with daily needs and toward seeking God’s kingdom first, which supports the prayer’s concern that life’s cares not displace spiritual concerns.

sections.heading: Responding to what you are doing in me
sections.text: Make me attentive to what you are teaching me through your dealings with me. When you correct me, do not let me ignore it. When you call me, do not let me stay unmoved. Give me a soft heart that receives your discipline, notices your mercy, and responds when you are leading me forward.
theological_themes: God uses correction and discipline to form his children.
Believers must respond to God’s work rather than becoming spiritually dull.
Providence should be received with humility and attentiveness.

scripture_references.connection: This passage presents the Lord’s discipline as fatherly love meant to produce holiness, supporting the prayer’s request to understand and respond rightly to God’s rebukes.
The proverb teaches that the Lord’s correction comes from love, helping frame the prayer’s desire not to be insensitive when God corrects.

sections.heading: Abiding in you while living in the world
sections.text: Teach me the holy skill of staying close to you. I live in this world, but do not let me belong to its values, loves, or false promises. Show me how to make every part of my life fit with faith in you—and more than that, how every part of my life can help me follow you more closely.
theological_themes: The Christian life depends on abiding in Christ.
Believers remain in the world but must not be shaped by its rebellion against God.
All of life can be received and ordered as service to God.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that fruitfulness depends on abiding in him, directly grounding the prayer’s final request to learn the art of remaining in God.
Jesus prays for his disciples to be kept from the evil one while being sent into the world, supporting the prayer’s desire to live in the world without belonging to it.
Paul calls believers to do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, which supports the prayer’s hope that every part of life can serve and strengthen faith.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The opening address, “Elector of saints,” reflects a Reformed doctrine of divine election. This is biblically grounded but doctrinally contested among Christians, so the adaptation preserves God’s initiative in calling without expanding into a full explanation of predestination.

The prayer strongly warns against false assurance and hypocrisy. The adaptation preserves that seriousness while avoiding language that would imply believers should seek assurance by introspection alone rather than by faith in Christ and the Spirit’s fruit.

The language of God’s “dealings,” “rebukes,” and “calls” assumes that God may use providence and discipline to correct and direct believers. This is biblical, but applying it to specific circumstances can be pastorally sensitive.
significant_interpretive_choices: I rendered “in the courts of heaven” and “in the dock of conscience” as God’s declaration of forgiveness together with a conscience given rest, preserving both the objective and subjective dimensions of assurance.
I interpreted “religion” in its older sense as the whole life of faith and devotion to God, not merely institutional practice or private spirituality.

I rendered “the holy art of abiding in thee” as learning to stay close to God and live every part of life in a way that supports faith, preserving the original’s practical and comprehensive vision of discipleship.
